analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal estate and generation-skipping inheritance taxes on large estates.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax was introduced in January 2019, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, which together tax the transfer of very large fortunes at death — in 2019, only estates above roughly $11 million per person ($22 million per couple) owed any estate tax at all. It would also change the gift tax so gifts given during life are taxed at flat rates rather than at estate-tax rates. The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates — those above roughly $11 million per person ($22 million per couple) — would keep the full value of their inheritance without federal estate tax. Wealthy families would also keep the ability to move money to heirs through gifts taxed only at low flat rates rather than estate-tax rates. Estate planning lawyers and wealth advisors who serve these families would keep a large fee base.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the estate tax, so heirs to large fortunes would owe nothing when inheriting — the tax previously applied to estates above roughly $11 million per person ($22 million per couple), affecting only the largest estates.
It repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which hits trusts set up to leave wealth to grandchildren, another tool affecting only very large estates.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would lose tens of billions of dollars of revenue per decade, made up through borrowing or higher taxes elsewhere. The burden falls on the general public, since the estate tax currently is paid only by the largest estates — nearly all of it by the top 1%.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate tax on large inherited wealth, which falls almost entirely on the estates of the wealthiest families; combined with keeping gift and income tax breaks, heirs of large fortunes would pay little or no tax on their inheritance.

The bill keeps the gift tax but only as a backstop at low flat rates, making it easier for wealthy families to shift assets to heirs before death with little tax — undermining the very tax base the gift tax was meant to protect.
Repealing the estate tax removes roughly tens of billions of dollars of federal revenue per decade, which either adds to deficits or must be made up by other taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — heirs of very large estates keeping tens of millions of dollars in taxes — is real but concentrated among a tiny number of families, while the cost (roughly $100+ billion in lost federal revenue over a decade, per general estimates) falls on everyone else through higher deficits or other taxes. Critics also note the name "Death Tax" mischaracterizes a tax that applies to very few, very large estates; the estate tax's already-high exemption meant only around 2 of every 1,000 estates owed it even before repeal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 116th Congress and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it expired with no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress, by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO).
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day — the only action it ever received.
No markup, vote, or further action followed before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill drew 128 cosponsors, 125 of them Republicans, showing strong backing within one party but no path to a floor vote with Democrats controlling the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families with large estates are better off because the bill died: the estate tax they would have faced on inheritances remains on the books.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 125 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, versus only 3 of 231 House Democrats, and with Democrats holding the House majority it never advanced.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and large family estates
industries.note: Heirs to estates above roughly $11 million per person would keep the entire inheritance tax-free. This is the bill's main constituency — it transfers money from the federal treasury to the richest few thousand families a year.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trust, and wealth management professionals
industries.note: The bill largely keeps the gift tax but restructures it, continuing work for lawyers and advisors who manage wealth transfers for rich families.
